\chapter{Saying and Seeing}
\label{ch:ar-saying-and-seeing}
\hlchaptermodality{29}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say the Arabic for 'he said' and 'he saw', read the letters qāf and alif maqṣūra, and name the doer, done-to, place and instrument words each root builds.}

Say raʾā, read its dotless alif maqṣūra, follow the root out into raʾy 'opinion' and mirʾāh 'mirror', and restate the pattern family qāla laid out.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[qāla]{\ar{قال} (qāla) — \textquotedblleft{}he said,\textquotedblright{} and a letter you have been reading unnamed}

\label{lesson:AR-C29-qala}



\begin{quote}
One letter has turned up in Arabic words since the farewell \emph{ilā l-liqāʾ} without ever being introduced. Its own verb is the right place to name it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The letters in this word}
One new letter, and it is a sound English does not have.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ق}} (\emph{qāf}) — \textbf{two dots above} a bowl-shaped body. Joined mid-word it looks much like \emph{bāʾ}'s bowl; alone or final it drops a deep round tail below the line. Its sound is a \emph{k} made far back at the \textbf{uvula}, at the top of the throat — heavier and darker than English \emph{k}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ا}} (\emph{alif}) and \textbf{\ar{ل}} (\emph{lām}) are yours already.
\end{itemize}

Read \textbf{\ar{قال}} right to left: \emph{qāf}, long \emph{ā}, \emph{lām}. Be honest about the sound: in most everyday spoken Arabic \textbf{\ar{ق}} is not said that way at all — in Cairo and Damascus it becomes a glottal stop, and across much of the Gulf a hard \emph{g}. The uvular version is the formal one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{قَالَ}} (\emph{qāla}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he said}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ق}-\ar{و}-\ar{ل}} — and the same disappearing act as \emph{jāʾa}, with the other weak letter. The plain shape would give \emph{qawala}; the \textbf{\ar{و}} dissolves and the vowel stretches to \textbf{ā}. It reappears the moment the pattern changes: \textbf{\ar{قَوْل}} (\emph{qawl}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{an utterance, a saying}.\textquotedblright{}

Now watch one skeleton fill four different pattern-slots:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{قَائِل}} (\emph{qāʾil}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{speaker},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{doer} shape.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَقُول}} (\emph{maqūl}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{spoken},\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{done-to} shape.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مَقالة}} (\emph{maqāla}) — \textquotedblleft{}an \textbf{article}, an essay,\textquotedblright{} the same \emph{ma-} place-and-way prefix that gave \emph{madhhab}.
\end{itemize}

Those first two are the very patterns met back in \emph{shukran}, which paired \emph{shākir} (\textquotedblleft{}thankful\textquotedblright{}) with \emph{mashkūr} (\textquotedblleft{}thanked\textquotedblright{}). Learn a pattern once and it works on every root — which is why Arabic vocabulary grows in families rather than one word at a time.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}qāla\textquotedblright{} — he said — with the deep uvular q
  \item the weak letter returning — qāla, then qawl, \textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — qāʾil, a speaker; maqūl, spoken; maqāla, an article
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many dots does \textbf{\ar{ق}} carry, and where is its sound made? (\textbf{Two, above} — at the \textbf{uvula}, far back in the throat.) Which letter of the root \textbf{\ar{ق}-\ar{و}-\ar{ل}} vanishes in \emph{qāla}, and which word brings it back? (\textbf{\ar{و}} — restored in \textbf{\ar{قَوْل}}, \emph{qawl}, \textquotedblleft{}a saying.\textquotedblright{}) What does \textbf{\ar{مَقالة}} mean, and which earlier word shares its pattern? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}An article\textquotedblright{}} — the same \emph{ma-} shape as \emph{\textbf{madhhab}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raʾā]{\ar{رأى} (raʾā) — \textquotedblleft{}he saw,\textquotedblright{} and how seeing becomes having an opinion}

\label{lesson:AR-C29-raa}



\begin{quote}
A weak letter has hidden in the middle of the last two verbs. This time it hides at the \textbf{end} — and it wears a shape of its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The letters in this word}
One new shape, and it is a shape you can almost already read.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{ر}} (\emph{rāʾ}) — the little downward curve, a tapped \emph{r}, and a non-joiner.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أ}} — \emph{alif} carrying \textbf{hamza}, the glottal catch, riding on top.
  \item \textbf{\ar{ى}} (\emph{alif maqṣūra}, \textquotedblleft{}the shortened alif\textquotedblright{}) — this is the new one, and it is simply \textbf{\ar{ي}} (\emph{yāʾ}) \textbf{stripped of its two dots}. Same body, no dots. Despite the \emph{yāʾ} body it sounds like a long \textbf{ā}, and it only ever turns up at the \textbf{end} of a word. The farewell \emph{ilā l-ghad} already carried it, unnamed.
\end{itemize}

Right to left: \emph{rāʾ}, then \emph{alif}-with-\emph{hamza}, then the dotless tail. \emph{Ra-ʾā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{رَأَى}} (\emph{raʾā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{he saw}.\textquotedblright{} Root \textbf{\ar{ر}-\ar{أ}-\ar{ي}}. The weak \textbf{\ar{ي}} is the \textbf{last} consonant this time, and instead of vanishing outright it surfaces as that dotless \textbf{\ar{ى}}. Three verbs, three placements of weakness: middle in \emph{jāʾa} and \emph{qāla}, final here. Each has its own regular rules.

The family this root grows is the good part:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{رَأْي}} (\emph{raʾy}) — \textquotedblleft{}an \textbf{opinion}.\textquotedblright{} Literally a \emph{seeing}. English does the very same thing with \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{in my view}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}the way \textbf{I see it}\textquotedblright{} — two unrelated languages reaching for one metaphor.
  \item \textbf{\ar{مِرْآة}} (\emph{mirʾāh}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{mirror}.\textquotedblright{} This is the \textbf{instrument} shape, \emph{mi-} plus the root: \textquotedblleft{}the thing you see with.\textquotedblright{} It is a sibling of the \emph{ma-} place shape behind \emph{madhhab} and \emph{maqāla}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{رُؤْيا}} (\emph{ruʾyā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{vision}, a dream.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Seeing, opinion, mirror, vision: four words, one skeleton, no memorising four unrelated forms.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}raʾā\textquotedblright{} — he saw — ending on a long ā spelled with a dotless yāʾ
  \item the metaphor — \textquotedblleft{}raʾy,\textquotedblright{} an opinion, literally a seeing
  \item the instrument — \textquotedblleft{}mirʾāh,\textquotedblright{} a mirror, the thing you see with
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\ar{ى}} made of, and what does it sound like? (\textbf{\ar{ي}} \emph{yāʾ} \textbf{without its dots} — sounding like a long \textbf{ā}, only ever at the end of a word.) What does \textbf{\ar{رَأْي}} mean, and what English turn of phrase makes the same move? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}An opinion\textquotedblright{}} — literally a seeing, like \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{in my view}.\textquotedblright{}) What is \textbf{\ar{مِرْآة}}, and what pattern builds it? (\textbf{A mirror} — the \emph{mi-} \textbf{instrument} shape, \textquotedblleft{}the thing you see with.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
